analogy.p: Picture walking along the edges of a polygon and turning at each corner. The angle you turn through at each corner is the exterior angle. When you get back to where you started, facing the way you began, you must have turned through exactly one full turn, 360°, however many corners there were. That is why a regular pentagon has exterior angles of 360° ÷ 5 = 72° and interior angles of 180° − 72° = 108°. It breaks down for a concave shape, because at a reflex corner you turn the other way, so the turns no longer all add in the same direction.

bullets: **Acute** angle: between 0° and 90° (less than a right angle).
**Right angle**: exactly 90°, marked with a small square in the corner; the two lines are **perpendicular**.
**Obtuse** angle: between 90° and 180°.
**Straight** angle: exactly 180°, which is simply a straight line.
**Reflex** angle: between 180° and 360°; a reflex angle is the 'outside' of a normal angle, so reflex = 360° − the angle on the other side.
**Three-letter notation**: ∠ABC (or angle ABC) is the angle at B. Always read the middle letter as the vertex.
Equal angles in a diagram are shown with matching arcs or ticks; a lower-case letter such as x is often used for an unknown angle.
Diagrams in exams are often marked **'not drawn accurately'**, so never measure from the diagram; work out angles using facts and reasons.
core.h: Types of angle and naming angles
core.p: An **angle** measures an amount of turn between two straight lines that meet at a point (the **vertex**). It is measured in **degrees** (°), where one full turn is 360°. Edexcel expects you to classify angles by size and to name them with the three-letter notation, so that there is no confusion about which angle a question means. The middle letter is always the vertex, so angle ABC is the angle at B between the lines BA and BC.

bullets: **Angles on a straight line add up to 180°.** If a ray splits a straight line into angles a and b then a + b = 180°.
**Angles around a point add up to 360°.** This works for any number of lines meeting at one point.
**Vertically opposite angles are equal.** When two straight lines cross, the angles directly opposite each other are equal; the neighbouring angles add to 180° (they are on a straight line).
Why vertically opposite angles are equal: if one angle is a, its neighbours on each side are 180° − a, and so the angle opposite is 180° − (180° − a) = a.
Several angles on one side of a straight line still add to 180° in total, e.g. 40° + 65° + x = 180° gives x = 75°.
The angle facts are used in the order: spot the fact, write the equation, solve, then state the reason in words next to your working.
core.p: Three facts underpin almost every angle question and each must be quoted exactly as the mark scheme words it. They all come from the idea that angles are shares of a turn. A straight line is half a turn (180°), a full turn is 360°, and when two straight lines cross they make two pairs of equal angles. Learn these as reasons, not just as numbers, because reasons earn marks in 'show that' and 'give a reason' questions.

bullets: **Equilateral** triangle: three equal sides and three equal angles of 60°.
**Isosceles** triangle: two equal sides; the two angles opposite the equal sides (the **base angles**) are equal. Reason: 'base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal'.
**Scalene** triangle: all sides and all angles are different.
**Right-angled** triangle: one angle of 90°, so the other two add up to 90°.
In an isosceles triangle with apex angle p the base angles are each (180° − p) ÷ 2; if one base angle is q, the apex angle is 180° − 2q.
The **longest side** is opposite the largest angle and the shortest side is opposite the smallest angle.

The **exterior angle of a triangle** (made by extending one side) equals the **sum of the two opposite interior angles**. Reason: the interior angle next to it is 180° minus it, and the three interior angles sum to 180°.
Sum of angles in a triangle: write the reason as 'angles in a triangle sum to 180°'.
core.p: The **angles in a triangle add up to 180°**. This is true for every triangle, whatever its shape or size, and it is the key fact from which the angle sums of all other polygons are built. Triangles are also classified by their sides and angles, and the special triangles carry extra angle facts that you can use immediately without proof. Recognising a hidden isosceles triangle (for example when two sides are radii of a circle or are marked equal) is one of the most common steps in multi-step problems.

bullets: **Square**: four equal sides, four right angles, diagonals equal and bisect at 90°.
**Rectangle**: opposite sides equal and parallel, four right angles, diagonals equal and bisect each other.
**Parallelogram**: opposite sides equal and parallel, **opposite angles equal**, co-interior angles add to 180°, diagonals bisect each other.
**Rhombus**: four equal sides, opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other at 90° and bisect the angles.
**Kite**: two pairs of adjacent equal sides, one pair of equal opposite angles, diagonals cross at 90°.
**Trapezium**: one pair of parallel sides; the angles between the parallel sides on the same leg add to 180°. An **isosceles trapezium** has equal base angles.
Reason to quote: 'angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360°'.
If a question gives three angles of a quadrilateral, the fourth is 360° minus their total.
core.h: Angles in quadrilaterals and their properties
core.p: A **quadrilateral** is a four-sided polygon and the **four interior angles add up to 360°**. You can prove this by drawing one diagonal, which cuts the quadrilateral into two triangles: 2 × 180° = 360°. The special quadrilaterals have further angle and side properties that mark schemes expect you to quote, and many questions give you a named shape and expect you to use its properties without being told.

bullets: **Corresponding angles are equal** (they sit in matching positions at the two intersections; the **F-shape**).
**Alternate angles are equal** (they lie on opposite sides of the transversal and between the parallel lines; the **Z-shape**).
**Co-interior angles add up to 180°** (they lie on the same side of the transversal and between the parallel lines; the **C or U-shape**). They are also called **allied** angles.
Why corresponding angles are equal: the second intersection is the first one translated along the transversal, so the angles are identical.
Why alternate angles are equal: an alternate angle is vertically opposite to a corresponding angle, so it is equal to it.
Why co-interior angles add to 180°: one is equal to the angle next to the other on a straight line, so together they make 180°.
**Converse**: if a pair of alternate or corresponding angles is equal, or co-interior angles add to 180°, then the lines must be parallel.
Always write the reason as e.g. 'alternate angles are equal' (or 'corresponding angles are equal'), never just 'Z angles'.
core.h: Parallel lines: the three angle pairs
core.p: **Parallel lines** are straight lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet; they are marked on diagrams with matching arrowheads. A line that crosses them is called a **transversal**. A transversal creates eight angles, and they come in just a few types. Each pair is recognised by a letter shape and you must use the exact name in your reason, because 'Z angles' or 'F angles' are not accepted by Edexcel mark schemes; use the full names **alternate**, **corresponding** and **co-interior**.

bullets: Label the triangle ABC. In the figure, a is the angle at A, c is the angle at B, and b is the angle at C.
Draw a line through C parallel to AB.
The angle between CA and the parallel line is equal to the angle at A because **alternate angles are equal**.
The angle between CB and the parallel line is equal to the angle at B because **alternate angles are equal**.
The three angles at C (a, b and c) make up the straight line through C, so they add up to 180° because **angles on a straight line sum to 180°**.
Conclusion: the angles of the triangle a + b + c = 180°.
Note that this proof works for **any** triangle, which is why a proof is stronger than checking one example with a protractor.
core.h: Proving the angle sum of a triangle
core.p: Edexcel Higher can ask you to **prove** results such as 'the angles in a triangle sum to 180°'. The standard proof uses parallel lines. Draw a line through one vertex that is parallel to the opposite side, then use alternate angles to bring all three interior angles together on a straight line. A proof must have every statement justified by a reason, and the final line must state the result that was to be proved.

bullets: Names by number of sides: 3 triangle, 4 quadrilateral, 5 pentagon, 6 hexagon, 7 heptagon, 8 octagon, 9 nonagon, 10 decagon.
An **interior angle** is inside the polygon at a vertex; an **exterior angle** is formed outside by extending one side.
A polygon with n sides can be split into **(n − 2) triangles** by drawing all possible diagonals from one vertex.
For a **regular** polygon every interior angle is equal and every exterior angle is equal; the shape also has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n.
A **convex** polygon has all interior angles less than 180°; a **concave** polygon has at least one reflex interior angle.
**Diagonals**: a line joining two non-adjacent vertices.
'Regular' must be stated or marked on the diagram before you may assume equal angles.
core.p: A **polygon** is a closed two-dimensional shape with straight sides. A **regular** polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal; an **irregular** polygon does not. You are expected to know the names of the common polygons, to recognise that a polygon with n sides also has n vertices and n interior angles, and to understand that a polygon can be split into triangles by drawing diagonals from a single vertex, which is the key to its angle sum.

bullets: Triangle (n = 3): 180°. Quadrilateral (n = 4): 360°. Pentagon (n = 5): 540°. Hexagon (n = 6): 720°.
Heptagon (n = 7): 900°. Octagon (n = 8): 1080°. Nonagon (n = 9): 1260°. Decagon (n = 10): 1440°.
Each interior angle of a **regular** polygon = (n − 2) × 180° ÷ n.
Regular values: triangle 60°, square 90°, pentagon 108°, hexagon 120°, heptagon 128.6° (3 s.f.), octagon 135°, nonagon 140°, decagon 144°.
To find the number of sides from a known interior angle of a regular polygon, solve (n − 2) × 180 = n × angle.
For an **irregular** polygon, add the known angles and subtract from the total to find the missing angle.
Check: the total must be a multiple of 180°; if it is not, there is an arithmetic error.
core.h: Sum of interior angles of a polygon
core.p: The **sum of the interior angles of an n-sided polygon is (n − 2) × 180°**. The reason is that the polygon can be split into (n − 2) triangles from one vertex and each triangle contributes 180°. This works for any polygon (regular or irregular, convex or concave). For a regular polygon, divide the total by n to find each interior angle. The reason to write in an exam is 'the interior angles of an n-sided polygon sum to (n − 2) × 180°'.

bullets: Exterior angle of a regular polygon = **360° ÷ n**, where n is the number of sides.
Number of sides of a regular polygon: n = 360° ÷ exterior angle. For example an exterior angle of 24° gives 360 ÷ 24 = 15 sides.
Interior angle = 180° − exterior angle.
Exterior angles of regular polygons: triangle 120°, square 90°, pentagon 72°, hexagon 60°, octagon 45°, decagon 36°.
For a regular polygon, 360° ÷ the exterior angle must be a whole number, because it equals the number of sides.
A regular polygon cannot have an exterior angle bigger than 120° (because it needs at least 3 sides).
Why the sum is 360°: the interior sum is (n − 2) × 180° and the n straight-line pairs total n × 180°, so the exterior sum is n × 180° − (n − 2) × 180° = 360°.
Reason to quote: 'the exterior angles of a polygon sum to 360°'.
core.p: At each vertex the interior and exterior angle lie on a straight line, so **interior angle + exterior angle = 180°**. The **sum of the exterior angles of any convex polygon is 360°**, whatever the number of sides. Imagine walking around the edge of the polygon: at each corner you turn through the exterior angle, and after going once round you have turned through exactly one full turn, 360°. For a **regular** polygon every exterior angle is the same, so each exterior angle is 360° ÷ n. This is usually the fastest way to find the number of sides.

bullets: Alternate or corresponding angles: **equate** the expressions, e.g. 3x + 10 = 5x − 30.
Co-interior angles or angles on a line: **add** the expressions and set equal to 180°.
Angles in a triangle: add all three expressions and set equal to 180°. Angles in a quadrilateral: set equal to 360°.
An isosceles triangle gives an equation with two equal expressions, e.g. 2x + 5 = 3x − 15.
After finding x, always substitute to give the **angle**, not just x, if the question asks for an angle.
Check that all the angles are positive and sensible; a negative or huge answer means an error.
Write the reason beside each equation, e.g. 'angles on a straight line sum to 180°'.
Practise expanding brackets and collecting like terms, as these are common slips in the algebra step.
core.p: Higher tier questions often give angles as algebraic expressions, so you have to form an equation from an angle fact and solve it. The method is always the same: decide which angle fact applies, write the expression sum or equality, solve the equation and then substitute back to find the angle values asked for. Check your answers by confirming that the angles satisfy the original fact, for example that the angles in a triangle really add up to 180°.

bullets: Common reasons: 'angles on a straight line sum to 180°', 'angles around a point sum to 360°', 'vertically opposite angles are equal'.
'Angles in a triangle sum to 180°', 'base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal', 'angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360°'.
'Alternate angles are equal', 'corresponding angles are equal', 'co-interior angles sum to 180°' (also accepted: allied angles).
'The interior angles of an n-sided polygon sum to (n − 2) × 180°', 'the exterior angles of a polygon sum to 360°'.
If you cannot see a route, try extending lines, drawing a line parallel to a given one, or marking all angles you can find; a diagram full of labels shows method marks.
Do not skip steps in 'show that' questions: every value must be justified and the answer given must match the one in the question.
Use the full word names; 'Z angles' or 'F angles' on their own may lose the reason mark.
core.h: Giving reasons and structuring multi-step problems
core.p: In 'work out the size of angle x, giving reasons for your answer' questions, each mark is usually for a correct angle value with a correct reason. The reason must be a recognised angle fact written in words. A good strategy is to find angles one at a time, label each on the diagram as you go, and write a short line such as 'Angle ABC = 180° − 65° = 115° (angles on a straight line sum to 180°)'. Start from angles that are given, work towards the one you need, and never rely on measuring.

bullets: **Circle theorems**: the radius to a tangent makes 90°, the angle in a semicircle is 90°, and the triangle formed by two radii is isosceles.
**Bearings**: parallel north lines create co-interior and alternate angles; the back bearing uses 180° ± the original.
**Tessellation**: regular triangles, squares and hexagons tessellate because 360° divides exactly by their interior angles (60°, 90°, 120°).
**Proof**: algebraic proofs such as 'prove the opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal' use parallel line facts.
**Algebra**: unknown angles in terms of x need forming and solving equations (including simultaneous equations at times).
**Similarity and congruence**: matching angles are used to prove two triangles similar.
**Trigonometry**: the sine and cosine rules need the angle sum of 180°.
**Polygons in 3D**: the faces of prisms and regular polyhedra use the same interior angles.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: Angle facts are used throughout GCSE Maths. In circle theorems the two radii of a circle make an isosceles triangle, so you use base angles equal. In bearings you use co-interior and alternate angles between north lines. In trigonometry and Pythagoras you find the right-angled triangle first. In transformations and tessellation, regular polygons tessellate only when their interior angles divide 360°. At Higher tier you will be asked to combine these facts into proofs.

exam: **1 mark** questions: state an angle fact or find an angle in one step, e.g. 'work out angle x'. Show the subtraction (180 − 65 = 115) in case of an arithmetic slip.
**'Give a reason'** (1 mark): write the fact in words, e.g. 'alternate angles are equal'. Use the exact names from the course.
**2 mark** questions: usually one angle with a reason, or two steps. M1 for a correct method, A1 for the correct value.
**3 to 4 mark** questions: a chain of two or three angles. Label each angle on the diagram and write each reason; award is for method, value and reasons.
**'Show that'**: every step must be written and justified, and you must end with the value given in the question.
**Proof questions** (usually 3 to 5 marks): state each fact with its reason, e.g. 'angle ABC = angle BCD because alternate angles are equal', and write a final concluding statement.
**Polygons**: if you are given an interior angle of a regular polygon, find the exterior angle (180 − angle), then n = 360 ÷ exterior angle.
**Algebra angle questions**: form the equation from the fact, solve for x, then substitute to give the angle; mark scheme: M1 equation, M1 solve, A1 answer.
Mark all the angles you find on the diagram; even partial working can earn method marks.
Check with a sense test: acute angles under 90°, obtuse over 90°, triangle total 180°.
Always include the degrees symbol in the final answer.

mistakes.r: Use the full names: 'alternate angles are equal', 'corresponding angles are equal', 'co-interior angles sum to 180°'.
mistakes.w: Writing 'Z angles' or 'F angles' as the reason

mistakes.r: Calculate using angle facts. Measured values earn no marks.
mistakes.w: Measuring angles from a diagram marked 'not drawn accurately'

mistakes.r: Co-interior angles add up to 180°; alternate and corresponding angles are the equal ones.
Each step needs a named angle fact in words next to the working.
mistakes.w: Giving the answer with no reason when 'give reasons' is asked

mistakes.r: That is the SUM of the interior angles. Divide by n for one angle of a regular polygon.
mistakes.w: Using (n − 2) × 180 as each angle of a polygon

mistakes.r: 360° ÷ n is the EXTERIOR angle. Interior = 180° − exterior.
mistakes.w: Using 360° ÷ n for the interior angle of a regular polygon

mistakes.r: Only use equal angles or sides if the question says regular or marks them equal.
mistakes.w: Assuming a polygon is regular when it is not stated

mistakes.r: Identify the two equal sides first, then the equal angles are opposite them.
mistakes.w: Forgetting that base angles of an isosceles triangle are the angles opposite the equal sides

mistakes.r: Substitute x back to give the actual angle if the question asks for an angle.
mistakes.w: Leaving the answer as x after solving an equation

summary: You must know and use the standard angle facts: angles on a straight line (180°), around a point (360°), vertically opposite angles, angles in triangles (180°) and quadrilaterals (360°), the three parallel-line angle pairs (alternate, corresponding, co-interior), and the interior and exterior angles of polygons including regular polygons. In Edexcel Higher you must give a correct reason for every step and combine facts into multi-step problems and algebraic proofs, so this topic underpins circle theorems, bearings, trigonometry and proof.

terms.d: A measure of turn between two lines that meet at a point, measured in degrees.
The point where two lines or sides of a shape meet.
An angle greater than 0° and less than 90°.
An angle greater than 90° and less than 180°.
An angle greater than 180° and less than 360°.
Lines that meet at a right angle (90°).
Angles opposite each other when two straight lines cross; they are equal.
Straight lines in the same plane that are always the same distance apart and never meet.
A straight line that crosses two or more other lines.
Equal angles on opposite sides of a transversal between two parallel lines (Z-shape).
Equal angles in matching positions at two intersections of a transversal with parallel lines (F-shape).
Angles on the same side of a transversal between parallel lines; they add up to 180° (C-shape). Also called allied angles.
A triangle with two equal sides and two equal angles (the base angles).
A closed 2D shape made of straight sides.
A polygon with all sides equal and all angles equal.
An angle inside a polygon at one of its vertices.
The angle between a side of a polygon extended and the next side; interior + exterior = 180°.
A line joining two non-adjacent vertices of a polygon.

worked.q: AB is parallel to CD. Angle PQB = (3x + 10)° and angle QRC = (5x − 30)°, and these two angles are alternate angles. (a) Work out the value of x. (b) Work out the size of angle PQB. Give a reason for your first step. (4 marks)
steps: Alternate angles are equal, so 3x + 10 = 5x − 30. [M1 equation, with reason: alternate angles are equal]

worked.q: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 156°. Work out the number of sides of the polygon. (3 marks)
steps: Exterior angle = 180° − 156° = 24° (interior and exterior angles lie on a straight line). [M1]
Sum of exterior angles of a polygon = 360°, so n = 360 ÷ 24. [M1]

worked.ans: 132° (reason: angles around a point sum to 360°)
worked.q: ABCDE is a regular pentagon and ABFGHI is a regular hexagon. They share the side AB and lie on opposite sides of AB. Work out the size of angle EAI, the angle at A not inside either shape. Give reasons. (3 marks)
steps: Interior angle of a regular pentagon = (5 − 2) × 180 ÷ 5 = 540 ÷ 5 = 108°. [M1]
Interior angle of a regular hexagon = (6 − 2) × 180 ÷ 6 = 720 ÷ 6 = 120°. [M1]
Angles around a point sum to 360°, so angle EAI = 360° − 108° − 120° = 132°. [A1]
